item.title: China urges Japan to deeply reflect on history of aggression: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China urges Japan to face up to and deeply reflect on its history of aggression, and gain the trust of its Asian neighbors and the international community with concrete actions, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a press briefing on Friday.
The September 18th Incident 95 years ago marked the start of Japan's 14-year invasion of China.
Ninety-five years ago today, Guo said, Japanese militarists launched aggression against China, and they were met by the courageous resistance of the Chinese people, which lifted the curtain of the eastern theater of the World Anti-Fascist War.
Noting the September 18th Incident was a war plot long concealed by the Japanese government from the Japanese public, Guo said the vast majority of the Japanese people did not learn the truth until the Tokyo Trials, which opened 80 years ago.
The increasingly prevalent historical denialism in Japan is truly troubling, and the danger is self-evident, Guo noted.
Denialism not just reflects serious regression in Japan's perception of history, but also indicates alarmingly an organized attempt to turn back the wheel of history with clear political motives, said Guo, adding that the real purpose is to keep the Japanese public from the truth, and clear the path for Japan to escape the straitjacket of the postwar system and rearm itself.
Denying the crime of aggression is to challenge historical conclusions and undermine the post-war international order, Guo said, stressing that all countries in the region, including China, must remain highly vigilant, not allow Japanese militarism to resurface, and not let historical tragedies repeat themselves.
"We must work together to uphold the outcomes of the World War II victory and jointly safeguard peace", Guo added.

item.title: 140th Canton Fair in south China to draw over 32,000 exhibitors
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- The 140th edition of the China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, will be held in three phases from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4 in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, with more than 32,000 companies set to participate, the Ministry of Commerce said on Friday.
Over the past seven decades, the Canton Fair has grown into China's largest and longest-running international trade fair, with the widest range of products, the largest number of buyers and the highest transaction volume, Zhang Li, assistant minister of commerce, said at a press conference.
China's trade in goods rose 17.6 percent year on year to 34.8 trillion yuan (about 5.15 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first eight months of 2026, with exports up 14.6 percent and imports increasing by 22 percent.
Zhang said China's foreign trade has shown stronger momentum in innovation and continued structural upgrading this year, trends also reflected at the Canton Fair.
Among the exhibitors, more than 11,000 are high-quality enterprises, including those that use specialized and sophisticated technologies to produce novel and unique products and those that hold leading positions in specific manufacturing segments, Zhang noted.
Roughly 64 percent of exhibitors use new technologies such as the industrial internet and artificial intelligence (AI), while new and green products will account for 23.2 percent and 26 percent of exhibits, respectively, with both shares reaching record highs.
This year's fair will further enhance its digital and intelligent operations by integrating technologies like AI and big data throughout the exhibition process, said Zhang.
It will introduce 22 smart application scenarios and 16 AI applications for the first time, and will be the first in China's exhibition industry to provide booth-level navigation across the entire venue and augmented reality displays of booth information.
Foreign trade companies are increasingly shifting from simply securing orders and selling products to building business systems and improving services. This year's fair will for the first time cover 10 categories of producer services in its trade services section, and 36.5 percent of exhibitors have shifted to a "product plus service" model, Zhang revealed.
More than 210,000 overseas buyers have so far completed pre-registration for this year's fair, with more expected to register as the opening date approaches.
This year marks the 70th anniversary of the Canton Fair, which has expanded from 9,600 square meters of exhibition space and 1,200 buyers at its inaugural session to 1.55 million square meters and around 310,000 buyers today.
The changing mix of products at the fair reflects the evolution of China's industrial structure. Agricultural and specialty products, handicrafts, textiles and light industrial goods featured prominently in its earlier years, before mechanical and electrical products became the fair's largest product category for the first time at its 86th session in 1999.
Today, the fair features products ranging from consumer electronics to new energy storage products, embodied intelligence products and smart medical equipment, with many cutting-edge Chinese-made products making their debuts at the event.
The Canton Fair has also served as a platform for Chinese foreign trade companies to enter and expand in international markets. From 1965 to 1979, annual exports generated through the fair accounted for more than 30 percent of China's total exports, exceeding 50 percent in some years, Zhang said.
Today, participating companies account for approximately 5 percent of China's foreign trade enterprises but contribute 16 percent of the country's general trade exports, according to Zhang.
Beyond securing orders, the fair also brings together the latest global market demand, consumer preferences, industry trends, product standards and application scenarios, Zhang said.

item.title: Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng to lead delegation to U.S. for trade talks on Sept. 19-23

item.title: Chinese premier chairs State Council executive meeting
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Friday chaired a State Council executive meeting, which heard a report on the work on population aging and discussed matters concerning the healthy development of sports events.
The meeting also made arrangements for the work to expand and upgrade medical rehabilitation and nursing care services, adopted a draft regulation on the protection of traditional knowledge of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), and discussed draft amendments to 15 laws.
Regarding the work on population aging, the meeting called for improving services and support for the elderly, and making sustained efforts in elderly care, health promotion and social security.
It also called for developing silver economy products and services tailored to the elderly, fostering new consumption scenarios, and better meeting elderly people's consumption needs.
On promoting the healthy development of sports events, the meeting stressed the need to increase the supply of high-quality sports events, make better use of various sports venues, facilities and event-related resources, and advance the coordinated development of competitive, professional and mass-participation sports events.
It also urged the integrated development of sports events with culture, tourism and commerce, faster application of new technologies, and improved spectator experience.
Regarding the sector of medical rehabilitation and nursing care, the meeting emphasized strengthening the service system with a focus on community-level services, extending rehabilitation and nursing resources to communities and families, and improving the accessibility of rehabilitation and nursing services for urban and rural residents.
It called for leveraging scientific and technological innovation to improve medical rehabilitation and nursing care, developing more intelligent technologies and equipment, optimizing the review and approval of new technologies and products, and enriching service scenarios.
The meeting also said that TCM theories, technologies and prescriptions are important resources for China's independent innovation. It called for comprehensively strengthening the protection and management of traditional knowledge of TCM to safeguard the foundation for the development of TCM, coordinating protection and utilization of TCM resources, and strengthening international exchanges.
The meeting discussed and approved, in principle, draft amendments to the 15 laws, including the Emergency Response Law, and decided to submit them to the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress for review.

item.title: Regional tensions put Saudi oil exports under pressure, rattle global energy markets
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
This photo taken on June 20, 2026 shows the Strait of Hormuz near Khasab, a small town in northern Oman. (Xinhua/Wen Xinnian)
RIYADH, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Escalating tensions across the Middle East are increasingly weighing on Saudi Arabia, one of the world's largest oil exporters.
As the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict continues to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, growing hostilities between Yemen's Houthi group and Saudi Arabia are also threatening Riyadh's oil export routes through the Red Sea, putting mounting pressure on Saudi Arabia's oil sector.
EASTERN ROUTE: HORMUZ TRAFFIC REMAINS SUBDUED
Like other major oil-exporting countries in the region, Saudi Arabia has traditionally shipped its crude oil from eastern ports into the Gulf and then through the Strait of Hormuz to international markets.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), an average of about 20 million barrels per day of crude oil and petroleum products passed through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025, accounting for roughly one quarter of global seaborne oil trade.
Since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes against Iran in February, Iran has effectively restricted traffic through the strait. The vital route remains far from normal to this day.
Recent data from maritime analytics firm Kpler highlights that only a handful of commodity-carrying vessels pass through the waterway daily, with a complete absence of Very Large Crude Carriers and Liquefied Natural Gas tankers on multiple days.
To mitigate the impact of disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia had begun exploring alternative export routes, including the East-West Pipeline, which transports oil to Yanbu Port on the Red Sea coast of western Saudi Arabia for shipment through the Red Sea.
Tanker carrying petroleum products navigates the Red Sea near the entrance of the Suez Canal in Suez Governorate, Egypt, on March 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)
WESTERN ROUTE: A "SAFETY VALVE" BECOMES A RISK POINT
However, Saudi Arabia's alternative western route for oil exports has also come under increasing constraints as the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi movement has intensified.
Accusing Saudi Arabia of violating areas under their control in Yemen, the Houthis announced on July 20 a maritime ban on Saudi vessels transiting the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The group subsequently claimed to have carried out attacks on Saudi vessels passing through the strait.
As the conflict between the two sides intensified, the Houthis began launching attacks against targets inside Saudi Arabia, including oil facilities.
The Saudi Ministry of Energy said on Sept. 11 that the East-West pipeline had come under multiple attacks in the Riyadh and Madinah regions, causing injuries. The pipeline was subsequently shut down as a precaution.
Analysts noted that the pipeline had previously served as a strategic "safety valve" for Saudi Arabia but had itself become a vulnerable point in the oil supply chain.
As of Sept. 16, Saudi authorities had not announced an official timetable for restarting the pipeline.
U.S. officials have suggested that flows could resume within "days," while Reuters reported that full repairs might take five to six weeks. Goldman Sachs said market estimates for the repair period ranged from a relatively quick recovery to as long as about eight weeks.
The more significant impact of such attacks was their effect on confidence in global oil markets. Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia could alter investors' assessments of the severity and duration of the conflict.
This handout photo provided by Houthi Media Center shows the launch of a missile allegedly toward Mocha in Yemen, on Aug. 9, 2026. (Houthi Media Center/Handout via Xinhua)
LONG-LASTING REPERCUSSIONS
Pressure on both of Saudi Arabia's major crude export routes has already begun to spill over into physical oil trading.
At the same time, the inventory "buffer" that has helped the global crude market absorb supply shocks is being eroded, shifting market attention toward when the entire supply chain, from oil fields and pipelines to storage facilities, ports and international shipping lanes, can return to stability.
IEA data showed that global observed oil inventories fell by another 95 million barrels in August. Since the end of February, inventories have declined by a cumulative 507 million barrels, equivalent to an average draw of roughly 2.8 million barrels per day.
Adam Ritchie, chief economist at Shell Trading, said in Oslo on Wednesday that since the escalation of the Middle East conflict, the global market had lost about 1.6 billion barrels of crude oil and condensates as well as roughly 36 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas supplies.
Rising transportation costs are adding to the pressure.
Paul Bradshaw, a director at Emirates National Oil Company, said that cargo insurance costs for some vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz had risen to 5 to 6 percent of cargo value, while additional war-risk premiums could reach as high as 10 percent.
Anders Opedal, chief executive officer of Norwegian energy company Equinor, said that if Middle Eastern supplies remain disrupted for an extended period, tighter energy markets and sharp price volatility could persist longer.

item.title: Remember history to safeguard peace
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
A ceremony to commemorate the September 18 Incident is held at the square of the 9.18 Historical Museum in Shenyang, northeast China's Liaoning Province, Sept. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Gang)
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- As air-raid sirens wailed in Chinese cities on Friday to commemorate the September 18 Incident, alarm bells should toll for a dangerous rise of Japanese neo-militarism today.
On Sept. 18, 1931, Japanese troops blew up a section of the railway near China's Shenyang city and later that night launched surprise attacks against Chinese military barracks in the city, marking the start of the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War.
Japan's imperialist aggression during World War II inflicted untold suffering on the people of China and the rest of the world. Remembering history is all the more relevant and necessary to cherish and safeguard peace today, as rising neo-militarism in Japan is posing a threat to world peace and stability again.
Over the years, Japanese right-wing forces have tried to break free from the postwar international arrangements. They have been trying every possible means to deny and distort history, and even whitewash the crimes committed during Japan's war of aggression, including revising history textbooks and indoctrinating the Japanese people with a wrong perception of history.
Japan has been accelerating its remilitarisation, drastically readjusting its security policy, increasing its defense spending for 14 consecutive years, relaxing its restrictions on lethal arms exports, developing and deploying offensive weapons, and going farther down the wrong path of military buildup. Its ambitions were laid bare when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi made remarks that implied the possibility of Japan's armed intervention in the Taiwan Strait in November last year.
Only by learning lessons from history can one avoid repeating mistakes. What Japan should do is to face up to its history of aggression, reflect on its war crimes, and make a complete break with militarism. This is the correct choice that serves the fundamental interests of the Japanese people.
Today's China is no longer what it was 95 years ago. The country has bid farewell to its old era of poverty and weakness and is advancing on its unstoppable course toward national rejuvenation. Its economic aggregate has ranked second in the world for years, and its people's armed forces have achieved leapfrog development, giving the nation solid confidence to safeguard peace.
Adhering to peaceful development, China will stand together with peace-loving countries in the world to firmly hold back the malevolent emergence of Japanese neo-militarism and prevent the tragedies of history from being repeated.

item.title: Xi Focus: Steering China's strides toward manufacturing powerhouse
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-19
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- Defying intense pressures at home and abroad, China's manufacturing sector has forged ahead, accelerating the construction of a modern industrial system with advanced manufacturing as its backbone, and solidifying the foundations for high-quality development.
China's manufacturing value-added accounts for nearly 30 percent of the global total, topping the world for over a decade.
That is no accident. It is the result of the insight and leadership of Chinese President Xi Jinping over the past years. As early as 2018, Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, said that China was experiencing a decline in manufacturing's share of the economy that was too fast, and the problem demanded close attention.
At a national conference on advanced manufacturing recently held in Beijing, Xi stressed the need to accelerate the development of a modernized industrial system with advanced manufacturing as its backbone and to reinforce the foundations of the real economy.
ANCHORING REAL ECONOMY
In May 2025, Xi visited Luoyang Bearing Group in Henan Province. Bearings are the joints of the entire manufacturing body, setting the performance ceiling for high-speed rail, wind turbines and aerospace alike.
Standing on the factory floor, Xi reflected on China's industrial journey. "From importing matches, soaps and iron products to becoming the world's largest manufacturing country with the most complete industrial sectors and categories, China has always adhered to the path of developing the real economy, which has proven to be the right path."
Over the years, Xi has walked the length and breadth of China's manufacturing landscape, and each stop has reinforced the same conviction that for a country of China's size, developing the real economy is non-negotiable.
At Gree Electric Appliances in 2018, he noted that advanced manufacturing is a key component of the real economy and that at no time should economic development become decoupled from the real economy and shift toward the virtual. At Zhengzhou Coal Mining Machinery the following year, he called manufacturing "the foundation of the real economy" and the real economy "the bedrock of the country's development." And at a "little giant" firm, Yangquan Valve, in 2025, Xi emphasized that the real economy should not be neglected, nor should the traditional industries within it.
Behind these instructions lies a profound reading of global economic history. International experience shows that manufacturing's share of GDP typically peaks and then declines as industrialization matures. When the decline goes too far, it hollows out industries and leaves an economy vulnerable to risks.
Under Xi's strategic vision, the country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) explicitly proposes moving faster to strengthen manufacturing, calling for maintaining a reasonable share of manufacturing in the economy and building a modern industrial system led by advanced manufacturing.
The president has also clarified the direction: high-end, intelligent, and green manufacturing.
China's manufacturing sector has been remarkably successful. In 2013, China sold just 17,600 new energy vehicles (NEVs), with market penetration at 0.08 percent. By 2025, annual sales had surged to 16.49 million units, with penetration reaching 47.9 percent.
In shipbuilding, China had held the top spot globally for 16 consecutive years by 2025, completing 56 percent of the world's ships and holding two-thirds of global orders last year. The same year, China's industrial robot exports grew 48.7 percent over 2024, surpassing imports for the first time and making China a net exporter of industrial robots.
BREAKING BOTTLENECKS THROUGH INNOVATION
While inspecting Wuhan HGLaser Engineering Co., Ltd. in June 2022, Xi attentively watched a display of innovative achievements in the chip industry and said earnestly: "With our country's further development, it is urgent to address the bottlenecks in core technologies in key fields."
For Xi, self-reliance and independent innovation are not slogans -- they are the fundamental guarantee for China's manufacturing to stand firm over the long run.
In the spring of 2023, a moment at the "two sessions," the annual meetings of China's top legislature and political advisory body, vividly showcased the confidence of China's manufacturing sector as it strides toward innovation and strength.
Shan Zenghai, a deputy from Xuzhou Construction Machinery Group (XCMG), a leading heavy machinery manufacturer, said that the company's 220-tonne all-terrain crane can now be 100 percent domestically produced, during a deliberation of deputies from Jiangsu Province.
"What about the chips in the cranes? Are they also homegrown?" Xi inquired.
The answer was affirmative. Shan said that XCMG manufactured 91 percent of all components in its products, up from 62 percent previously. Xi commended the company's achievements in making world-class engineering machinery. "We need to upgrade to medium- and high-end manufacturing. This is a hallmark of high-quality development."
The Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee has repeatedly dedicated study sessions to frontier technologies. Concrete measures have followed. China has established national manufacturing innovation centers, launched major science and technology projects, rolled out a decade-long action plan for basic research, and focused on full-chain breakthroughs in critical sectors, including integrated circuits and industrial machine tools.
In the first half of this year, China's major industrial enterprises produced 279.8 billion integrated circuit units, surging 23.1 percent year on year.
POWERING THE WORLD
From solar panels harvesting sunlight in Egypt's deserts to China-Europe freight trains carrying equipment across Eurasia, China's manufacturing has become deeply embedded in global supply chains, powering the world with affordable, high-quality products and technologies.
"As we further modernize our industrial system, we will provide the world with more and better products made and created in China, and with a Chinese market of a larger scale and stronger demand," Xi said at a meeting in 2023.
This pledge is being translated into concrete action. Today, China has fully eliminated market access restrictions for foreign investment in the manufacturing sector. The updated catalog of encouraged foreign investment industries channels foreign capital into advanced manufacturing and other high-end fields, while international standards exchanges in areas such as NEVs and artificial intelligence continue to deepen.
As the world's largest manufacturing country, China has built extensive, well-integrated production capacity across a wide range of industrial goods, allowing producers worldwide to access key equipment, components and intermediate goods at lower cost and with greater efficiency.
Through technological innovation and intense market competition, China has built the world's largest and most integrated supply chains for the new energy industry. Chinese solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and NEVs have made energy transition more affordable.
Attending the BRICS summit in New Delhi last week, Xi proposed five initiatives, including an intelligent manufacturing cooperation initiative. He said China stands ready to help fellow BRICS countries build smart factories, develop standards and norms, and jointly promote manufacturing transformation and upgrading.
Experts noted that Chinese products have won markets with their proven strength, and Chinese manufacturing has built deep confidence with its remarkable resilience. This is a powerful testament to the strategic vision of developing advanced manufacturing, and a vivid display of the broad horizons of innovation-driven progress.

item.title: Beyond expo floor, AI opens new frontiers in China-ASEAN cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
*China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) both aim to expand AI's role in bilateral trade, which exceeded 1 trillion U.S. dollars last year.
*In the first seven months of 2026, China-ASEAN trade rose 24.7 percent year on year to 744.41 billion dollars, Chinese customs data show, as AI use expands in marketing, agriculture, logistics and finance.
*The distinction between technology that draws a crowd and technology that delivers real value is central to the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo and the China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit, slated from Sept. 17 to 21 in Nanning, Guangxi's capital.
NANNING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Wei Qiaomei, a Chinese livestreamer, once struggled to grasp what her Thai customers wanted, though she speaks fluent Thai.
Once, ahead of her pitch for a portable fan, AI analyzed Thai e-commerce data and popped up two selling points for her: quiet motors and long battery life.
The trial has proven rewarding. Her employer, based in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, reported a 300 percent sales jump.
"Speaking the language isn't the same as understanding the market," said the 23-year-old, noting that AI had transformed her from a mere translator into a market-savvy presenter.
Her story reflects a broader shift in relations between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), as both sides aim to expand AI's role in bilateral trade, which exceeded 1 trillion U.S. dollars last year.
This photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows a view of the Nanning International Convention and Exhibition Center, the venue for the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo, in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.(Xinhua/Zhou Hua)
FROM SHOWCASE TO APPLICATION
The event brings together more than 3,400 companies, with Timor-Leste attending for the first time as ASEAN's 11th member and an official co-host.
The expo's inaugural "AI marketplace" features about 500 products from more than 70 companies across eight categories, such as wearables, health management, and consumer technology, allowing visitors to test and buy items on-site.
"Last year, AI was mostly for show. This year, it is driving sales," said Wang Jicai, secretary-general of the China-ASEAN Expo Secretariat.
For Wei, the results are clear. Her company trained its model on ASEAN languages, local preferences, and cultural nuances, enabling it to analyze products, process reviews, and draft localized scripts. Livestream hosts then decide when to pivot, how to handle tough questions, and what to emphasize.
"AI didn't replace me. It amplified what I could do," Wei said.
Beyond the livestream studio, AI applications are being deployed in several ASEAN markets.
In Laos and Cambodia, a platform developed by a Guangxi enterprise and local partners uses satellite imagery, drones, and ground sensors to track pests and guide tropical crop cultivation.
The system, built with Chinese technology, local field data and training support, has been tested on more than 20,000 mu (about 1,333 hectares) of crops, said project head Wen Biaotang.
Visitors take photos of a humanoid robot performing tea ceremony during the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhou Hua)
CROSS-BORDER DEPLOYMENT NARROWS AI DIVIDE
In Guangxi's border city Chongzuo, the center for disease control and prevention has partnered with neighboring Vietnamese provinces to deploy a bilingual AI platform for early disease detection.
It can slash epidemiological reporting time from four hours to 30 minutes, the project manager said.
In Nanning, RunDo, a platform operated by Runjian Co. Ltd., monitors almost 300 megawatts of solar capacity across nearly 3,000 sites in Malaysia remotely, with drones and AI replacing manual inspections.
"The platform has boosted maintenance efficiency by over 30 percent, raised power output by up to 5 percent, and cut labor costs by more than 20 percent," said Yang Yexi, marketing manager of the operator's Guangxi branch.
Leveraging Nanning's computing infrastructure, ASEAN companies can avoid building large intelligent computing centers and remotely access models and computing power for their business needs, Yang said, whose company has launched more than 80 computing projects across ASEAN.
These cases highlight the prerequisites for cross-border AI deployment: computing power, local data, skilled workers, and capable local partners.
Guangxi's China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center has cataloged more than 1,000 potential AI scenarios, opened 279 to developers, set up offices in Vietnam, Laos, and Malaysia, backed more than 30 cross-border projects, and assembled an alliance of 55 companies.
To address the low-resource challenge faced by some Southeast Asian languages, a training base in Malaysia has logged more than 1,900 hours of multilingual data annotation, while a six-month regional competition attracted more than 200 teams.
Liu Jianmin, a professor at the School of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence of Guangxi University of Finance and Economics, said ASEAN universities, companies, and professionals could contribute to collecting, labeling and updating data if AI models are to work locally.
"No matter how accurate a system is, if no one uses it, can afford it, or can keep it running, it remains just an exhibit," Liu said.
The challenge is acute for ASEAN's smaller economies.
Without collective action, the cost of cybersecurity, data governance, and reliable AI frameworks could deepen an "intelligence divide," said Miguel Marques Goncalves Manetelu, Timor-Leste's minister of transport and communications.
This photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows a scene of the opening ceremony of the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo and China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming)
FROM MATCHMAKING TO RULE-MAKING
Before the expo opened, an AI system had generated more than 8,000 buyer-seller matches and arranged nearly 2,000 face-to-face meetings.
According to the summit's organizers, the system provides real-time tariff and compliance guidance during negotiations, and tracks leads after the exhibition.
But, it still can not establish cross-border data protocols, guarantee electronic signatures, or assign liability when an algorithm fails.
AI can turn industrial expertise into a service that can be sold and delivered over time, said Meng Shuang, an associate professor of international economics at the Central University of Finance and Economics in Beijing.
Companies, she said, will increasingly package hardware, software, models, and long-term maintenance, with competitive advantage extending to algorithms, sector expertise, and local operating ability.
This evolution has pushed regional trade into more complex territory: data governance, AI service pricing and billing rules, electronic authentication, and intellectual property.
"Cross-border data flows are the lifeblood of AI," said ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn, who called for a trusted, secure, and seamless framework for data exchange.
The China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, signed in October 2025, sets out a regional framework covering the digital and green economies, cross-border data flows, personal privacy, digital payments, and AI standards.
Standardized electronic authentication, interoperable payments, and joint data frameworks would first benefit sectors such as cross-border e-commerce, smart logistics, and industrial inspection, Meng added.
Ge Hongliang, a researcher at the School of Southeast Asian Studies at Guangxi Minzu University, said that cooperation among free-trade zones and ports under the upgraded protocol could support investment, data sharing, and intellectual-property protection.
To that end, this year's expo is hosting its first high-level dialogue on aligning Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and China-ASEAN FTA rules.
For livestreamers like Wei, it comes down to knowing which fan feature matters most to a customer hundreds of miles away.

item.title: Pinglu Canal's Madao Hub Showcases Smart, Green Ship Locks
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
A new gateway from China's inland waterways to the sea!
The Madao hub on the Pinglu Canal in Guangxi features giant water-saving locks and smart monitoring systems.
The 134.2-km canal will connect China's inland waterways with the Beibu Gulf, creating a shorter, more efficient route to the sea.
